opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that autonomous driving is a much more constrained problem, even though it's still very hard. A car essentially does two things: it controls direction and speed. The road is structured, with lanes, traffic lights, rules and signs, and the whole society has spent a hundred years building infrastructure around the car. So the action space is relatively small, and the environment, while complex, is fairly well defined.

A general-purpose robot is a completely different story. It has to work in open, unstructured environments like homes, factories and hospitals, where every space is different. It has to manipulate objects of all kinds of shapes, weights and materials, which requires fine-grained dexterity, tactile sensing and force control. A humanoid robot has dozens of degrees of freedom. The physics of grasping a soft towel versus an egg versus a cup of hot water is much harder to model than keeping a car in its lane.

The second reason is data. Autonomous driving has a huge data advantage. There are hundreds of millions of cars on the road, many already equipped with cameras and sensors, so you can collect enormous amounts of real-world driving data, and the data format is fairly uniform. For robotics, we don't have that kind of data flywheel yet. Robot hardware is diverse, the tasks are diverse, and collecting high-quality interaction data is expensive and slow. That's why people are working so hard on simulation, teleoperation and learning from human video. But it's still early.

Third, the business model and value chain are much clearer for driving. Robotaxis, trucking, logistics and assisted driving in private cars all have clear customers and clear economics. In China, robotaxi fleets are already operating in many cities, and the cost of the vehicles and sensors has come down dramatically. For general-purpose robots, the hardware is still expensive, reliability isn't there yet, and it's not clear what the first killer application at scale will be.

So my view has been that autonomous driving is the first large-scale deployment of physical AI, of embodied intelligence. You can think of an autonomous vehicle as a robot on wheels, the first robot that truly enters everyday life at scale. Much of what we learn from it, including the perception, the end-to-end models, the world models, the safety validation and the regulatory frameworks, will carry over to robotics. Then, I believe, general-purpose robots will follow, perhaps starting with more structured settings like factories and warehouses before eventually reaching homes. But that is a longer journey, maybe another five to ten years beyond where autonomous driving is today.

r001.rationale: It says autonomous driving is a more constrained problem, with structured roads and a relatively small action space, unlike general-purpose robots’ open environments and varied tasks.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes an autonomous vehicle as “a robot on wheels,” framing autonomous driving as a specialized form of robotics.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simplest way I put it is this: a car is a robot, but it's a robot with a very narrow job. It operates in a structured environment. There are lanes, there are traffic rules, there are signals, there's a road network that was designed over a hundred years for machines to move on. The task is essentially one thing, get from A to B safely, and the degrees of freedom are quite limited. You control steering, acceleration, braking. That's it. A humanoid or a general-purpose robot has dozens of degrees of freedom, it has to manipulate objects, it has to deal with a kitchen, a hospital, a warehouse, each one completely different, and there's no standardized environment waiting for it.

The second reason is data. For autonomous driving we already have enormous amounts of real-world data. Tesla has billions of miles, Waymo has tens of millions of fully autonomous miles, and every car on the road with sensors is collecting more. For robots, the embodied data basically doesn't exist yet at that scale. People are trying with teleoperation, with simulation, with video, but it's early. I always say that in AI you need the algorithm, the compute, and the data, and for driving all three are now in place.

The third reason is commercial. The car industry is a trillion-dollar industry with mature supply chains, mature regulation, and customers who already pay for the product. So when you add autonomy, you're adding a capability to something that already works economically. Robotaxis are already running commercially in San Francisco, in Phoenix, in Wuhan, in Beijing. That's not a demo anymore. General-purpose robots still have to prove what job they do and who pays for them.

So I think of it as a sequence. Autonomous vehicles are the first large-scale embodied AI, really the first robot that billions of people will interact with. What we learn there, the perception, the planning, the end-to-end models, the safety validation, the regulatory frameworks, all of that becomes the foundation for broader robotics. My own view is that in the next three to five years, Level 4 driving becomes mainstream in major cities, and general-purpose robots in homes probably take another five to ten years beyond that. The order isn't a coincidence. The simpler, more constrained, more data-rich problem gets solved first.

r001.rationale: It says driving has a narrow, structured task with limited degrees of freedom, while general-purpose robots face varied environments and tasks.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes a car as a robot with a very narrow job.

astra-6.text:
I think autonomous driving will be deployed earlier because it is a more clearly defined problem. Driving is very difficult, but the objective is specific: get from one place to another safely. The vehicle operates on roads, follows traffic rules, and has a relatively limited set of actions—steering, braking, and acceleration. You can also begin deployment in a restricted area and under particular conditions, then expand gradually.

A general-purpose robot has to deal with much more variety. If you ask a robot to help around the house, it needs to understand your intention, navigate an unfamiliar environment, recognize objects, and manipulate them. Picking up a glass and folding a shirt require very different capabilities. The physical interaction is especially challenging.

So it’s not that autonomous driving is easy. It’s that we can constrain the problem and build a useful service within those constraints. General-purpose robots need a much broader combination of intelligence, dexterity, and reliability.

r001.rationale: It says driving has a specific objective, operates under road rules with limited actions, and can be deployed in restricted conditions, unlike the varied demands of general-purpose robots.

r002.rationale: It describes autonomous driving as a bounded task but does not characterize it as a specialized form of robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think autonomous driving is a more constrained problem. The car operates on roads, follows traffic rules, and has a relatively limited set of actions: steering, accelerating, and braking. Of course, handling all the unexpected situations safely is still very difficult, but the task itself is well defined.

A general-purpose robot has to work in a much less structured environment. Even something as simple as cleaning a kitchen requires recognizing many different objects, understanding what needs to be done, and manipulating things with different shapes, weights, and materials. It needs both intelligence and very capable physical hardware.

So I expect autonomous driving to be deployed first, especially within defined areas and operating conditions. General-purpose robots will take longer, although robots designed for specific tasks can arrive much sooner.

r001.rationale: It says autonomous driving is more constrained and well defined than general-purpose robotics, which must operate in less structured environments.

r002.rationale: It discusses autonomous driving as a constrained car task but does not characterize it as a form of robotics.
